To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a mechanistic, dynamic model of disease transmission in wildlife can be used to predict disease dynamics and that tuberculosis can be maintained in a white-tail deer population for >15 yr without maternal transmission.

a mechanistic model of tuberculosis transmission in a dynamic host population predicted that tuberculosis prevalence would rise from 3% to 21% in a white-tail deer population over 25 yr and that neither lowered survival nor lowered transmission was likely to be completely effective in controlling the epidemic.
a mechanistic model of disease transmission in dynamic populations can forecast tuberculosis dynamics in white-tailed deer populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and applying a model that can be used to forecast tuberculosis transmission in wildlife populations.

the development of a general model that can be applied to any disease system in a dynamic host population, and the use of the model to forecast the possible outcome of a tuberculosis epidemic in white-tailed deer.
the application of a general model of disease transmission in dynamic wildlife populations to a specific disease (M. bovis) and host (deer) population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a disease such as bovine tuberculosis, which has a high prevalence among cattle and which is capable of being transmitted to deer, could be expected to persist in a deer population.
a tuberculosis epidemic in a white tailed deer population is possible, but not inevitable, and that the disease is likely to be sustained in the population by lateral transmission.

the disease would be eliminated in a deer population if lateral transmission were eliminated, but the time required for this to occur would be long and would depend on the initial disease prevalence and the survival rate of deer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a mechanistic approach to modeling disease transmission in wildlife populations can be useful in understanding the potential for disease spread, in forecasting possible epidemic trajectories, and in evaluating the effectiveness of disease-control measures.
tuberculosis in a white-tail population would not be self-limiting, and that eradication of the disease would require a sustained effort to control both deer survival and transmission.
a tuberculosis epidemic is possible in white-tailed deer, and that it could be difficult to eliminate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the model we developed is flexible, and can be adapted to a wide variety of host-pathogen systems.
the dynamics of wildlife disease can be modeled in a flexible and mechanistic manner.
wildlife disease dynamics may be forecasted by using a mechanistic approach, even in the absence of detailed data on disease transmission.
